sections.heading: Exports

FiveM has native resource exports, so getResource() remains the normal path for direct resource access.
OpenCore also exposes an optional explicit remote export helper layer for consistency with other adapters and for teams that prefer an async-only calling style: Use guidance:

sections.heading: Manual loading screen shutdown
sections.content:
FiveM supports loadscreenmanualshutdown 'yes' for flows where the world should remain hidden until the client has prepared its scene.
OpenCore supports this in the spawn lifecycle through skipLoadingScreenShutdown.
Server-side: Client-side: Use this when you need to:
spawn at a neutral staging position
load models or animation dictionaries
configure cinematic cameras
reveal the world only after the scene is ready
When skipLoadingScreenShutdown is set, OpenCore does not call ShutdownLoadingScreen

title: Adapters

sections.heading: What are Adapters?
sections.content: Adapters are packages that connect OpenCore with specific multiplayer platforms. Each adapter implements the framework's contracts for platform-specific APIs like player info, vehicle management, events UI bridges and extra APIs.

sections.heading: Available Adapters
sections.content: Adapter Package Status Game FiveM @open-core/fivem-adapter Stable GTA V RageMP @open-core/ragemp-adapter Stable GTA V RedM Built-in Coming Soon RDR3

sections.heading: Common Contracts
sections.content: All adapters implement these core contracts:

sections.heading: Server Contracts
sections.content:
IPlayerServer — Player operations (drop, getPed, getName, getPing)
IVehicleServer — Vehicle operations (create, delete, getAll)
IPedServer — Ped operations (spawn, delete)
IPlayerLifecycleServer — Spawn, teleport, respawn actions
IPlayerStateSyncServer — Health, armor, state sync
IPlatformContext — Platform info and capabilities
MessagingTransport — RPC and events between server/client

sections.heading: Client Contracts
sections.content:
IClientRuntimeBridge — Tick, commands, NUI callbacks
IClientSpawnBridge — Player spawn management
IClientWebViewBridge — WebView/NUI communication
IClientBlipBridge — Map blip management
IClientMarkerBridge — 3D marker rendering
IClientNotificationBridge — Notifications and help text

sections.heading: Installation
sections.content:
Each adapter has its own package. Install the ones you need:
```bash

sections.heading: FiveM
sections.content: pnpm add @open-core/fivem-adapter

sections.heading: RageMP
sections.content:
pnpm add @open-core/ragemp-adapter
```

sections.heading: Validating Adapter Coverage
sections.content:
If you maintain an adapter package, use the CLI helper command to verify that your adapter still covers the framework contracts expected by OpenCore:
```bash

sections.heading: run inside the adapter repository
sections.content: opencore adapter check

sections.heading: fail on optional parity gaps too
sections.content:
opencore adapter check --strict
``
The command compares your adapter's server and client bindings against the framework's default adapter baseline.
It is useful when:
new contracts are added to the framework
you are upgrading @open-core/framework
you want a fast verification step in CI for adapter packages
By default the report separates:
required contracts that must exist for the adapter to pass
optional parity gaps that are reported as warnings unless --strict` is used

CLI Commands

sections.heading: Exports
sections.content:
OpenCore keeps @Export() as the public programming model and the adapter provides two layers:
Local registry access for synchronous framework internals such as core.isCoreReady()
An optional explicit remote export transport for server resource-to-resource calls
Use the framework contract instead of reaching into exportsRegistry directly:

sections.heading: API Summary
sections.content:
getResource(resourceName) Use for local/synchronous resolution. This is what the framework uses internally for CORE bootstrap and provider lookups.
getRemoteResource(resourceName) Returns an async proxy when you want explicit remote resource calls.
callRemoteExport(resourceName, exportName, ...args) Calls one remote export explicitly.
waitForRemoteResource(resourceName, options) Waits until a resource exposes a specific export before returning the async proxy.

sections.heading: Security Notes
sections.content:
Remote exports are server-side only.
The adapter executes only methods registered through @Export().
Client-originated payload shapes are ignored by the remote export transport.
Treat remote export helper calls as async RPC, not as direct shared-memory calls.
--

sections.heading: Node 14 dependency compatibility
sections.content:
RageMP server runtimes commonly run on Node Some modern packages may declare compatible engines and still fail at runtime because their transitive dependencies use newer Node features such as node: specifiers.
This affects packages like ORMs, database drivers, file globbers, and build-time tooling that may also execute during server bootstrap.
Recommendations:
Prefer explicit versions for critical runtime dependencies such as typeorm, pg, and similar infrastructure packages. Tested versions: typ

sections.heading: Misleading autoload errors
sections.content:
If you see a message like: it may actually be a nested dependency failure triggered while importing the autoload module.
Check the full stack trace and verify the dependencies imported by your controllers before assuming the autoload file itself is missing.

title: Benchmark Strategy & Results

sections.heading: Benchmark Strategy & Results
sections.content:
OpenCore benchmarks are organized around engineering value.
The goal is not to collect impressive microbenchmark numbers. The goal is to answer questions that matter to real multiplayer servers:
What does a full command path cost?
What does a validated net event cost?
What happens under concurrency pressure?
How expensive is startup as the controller graph grows?
What tick budget is consumed as handlers and work increase?

sections.heading: Gold
sections.content:
These are the default product-facing benchmarks.
full command execution
full net event handling
RPC paths
player lifecycle churn
tick budget impact
binary transport paths

sections.heading: Startup
sections.content:
These measure framework boot and registration cost.
metadata scanning
dependency injection setup
schema generation
bootstrap controller registration

sections.heading: Diagnostic
sections.content:
These are lower-level framework internals.
Zod validation internals
rate limiter internals
access control internals
event bus internals
metadata and decorator cost
These are useful for maintainers, but they are not the main benchmark story for production servers.

sections.heading: Soak
sections.content: Longer-running stress scenarios for stability and degradation checks.

sections.heading: Latest Run
sections.content:
Source:
Framework version: 1.0.6
Report timestamp: 2026-04-01T19:03:36.782Z

sections.heading: Commands
sections.content:
Scenario Throughput p95 -- -- -- Command Full Validated (100 players) 115.68K ops/sec 0.012ms Command Full End-to-End (100 players) 863.50K ops/sec 0.0027ms Command Full Concurrent (100 players) 121.71 ops/sec 14.42ms Takeaway:
validated command handling is cheap
contention changes the picture much more than validation itself

sections.heading: Net Events
sections.content:
Scenario Throughput p95 -- -- -- Net Events Validated (10 players) 9.61K ops/sec 0.488ms Net Events Full Event (small, 10 players) 74.42K ops/sec 0.029ms Net Events Full Event (medium, 10 players) 44.73K ops/sec 0.079ms Net Events Full Event (large, 10 players) 27.68K ops/sec 0.113ms Takeaway:
payload size matters
validation remains affordable

sections.heading: RPC
sections.content:
Scenario Throughput p95 -- -- -- RPC Schema generation simple (200 methods) 7.95K ops/sec 0.176ms RPC Schema generation complex (200 methods) 3.06K ops/sec 0.400ms Takeaway:
schema complexity is a real startup and registration cost

sections.heading: Player Lifecycle
sections.content:
Scenario Throughput p95 -- -- -- Full Cycle (500 players) 200.55K ops/sec 0.0096ms Concurrent Connections (500 players) 108.68K ops/sec 0.0046ms Concurrent Disconnections (500 players) 1.83M ops/sec 0.00075ms Takeaway:
lifecycle churn scales well
connect cost is meaningfully higher than disconnect cost

sections.heading: Tick Budget
sections.content:
Scenario Throughput p95 -- -- -- Tick Real setTick (50 handlers) 93.12K ops/sec 0.021ms Tick 5 Handlers (medium workload) 18.45K ops/sec 0.098ms Tick 5 Handlers (heavy workload) 2.26K ops/sec 0.559ms Tick Parallel Execution 243.24 ops/sec 8.00ms Takeaway:
small handlers are cheap
heavy work inside ticks is dangerous
parallel tick execution is not a free win

sections.heading: BinaryService
sections.content:
Scenario Throughput p95 -- -- -- Parse mixed responses (500 ops) 1.20M ops/sec 0.0011ms Full round-trip (50 calls) 350.12K ops/sec 0.0092ms Serialize large payload (500 ops) 2.88K ops/sec 0.428ms Takeaway:
binary transport is strong for parse and round-trip
large payload serialization is the expensive path

sections.heading: Startup Results
sections.content:
Scenario Throughput p95 / p99 -- -- -- Bootstrap 100 controllers 205.87 ops/sec p95 6.37ms MetadataScanner 10 controllers 112.61K ops/sec p99 21.15μs DI Resolve simple service 1.92M ops/sec p99 1.36μs SchemaGenerator batch 50 methods 628 ops/sec p99 14.17ms Takeaway:
startup remains healthy overall
schema generation is the main startup hotspot in this run

sections.heading: What This Means For Servers
sections.content:
The framework is fast on validated happy paths.
The real costs show up under contention, not in single-path microbenchmarks.
Tick work and large payload serialization deserve the most operational attention.
Startup cost is acceptable and mostly scales with schema generation and registration volume.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
Results are hardware-dependent.
Compare runs relatively, not absolutely.
gold should be the main suite used to talk about framework performance.
diagnostic is still useful, but it is not the product-facing benchmark story.

title: Performance & Compute

sections.heading: Principles
sections.content:
OpenCore performance comes from predictable pipelines, explicit boundaries, and lightweight handlers.
Keep these priorities:
Validate early, fail fast.
Keep tick handlers tiny.
Use interval/event-driven flows over per-frame logic.
Keep heavy CPU work outside the main loop.

sections.heading: Server Guidelines
sections.content:
Prefer Interval/event handlers over continuous OnTick loops.
Avoid expensive synchronous loops in command/net handlers.
Cache immutable lookups where possible.
Use squared-distance checks for spatial filters when feasible.

sections.heading: Client Guidelines
sections.content:
Minimize native calls in every frame.
Batch UI updates and avoid chatty WebView messages.
Use StreamingService and model preloading to avoid spikes.

sections.heading: Parallel Compute
sections.content:
Use ParallelCompute for CPU-heavy pure JS/TS operations. It can run sync, worker, or distributed modes based on cost thresholds.
Typical candidates:
Large list transforms
Expensive spatial sorting/filtering
Non-native data processing tasks

sections.heading: Measure First
sections.content:
Profile before optimizing.
Track p95 latency for handlers, not only averages.
Validate gameplay impact (server tick stability, client FPS, input responsiveness).

sections.heading: Benchmark Strategy
sections.content:
OpenCore now separates benchmarks by engineering value:
gold: real framework feature paths
startup: boot and registration cost
diagnostic: low-level internals for maintainers
soak: longer-running stress checks
The full benchmark strategy and latest validated results live here:
Benchmark Strategy & Results

sections.heading: Practical Summary
sections.content:
The current benchmark runs show a few clear rules:
validated command and event paths are cheap
contention is more dangerous than validation overhead
heavy tick work is one of the easiest ways to hurt server responsiveness
large payload serialization is a much bigger cost than small or medium payload paths
startup cost is mostly visible in schema generation and controller registration scale

title: Scaling Resources (CORE ↔ RESOURCE)

sections.heading: Goal
sections.content: Scale by separating authoritative runtime responsibilities (CORE) from feature resources (RESOURCE) while keeping one programming model.

sections.heading: Recommended Topology
sections.content:
CORE resource: player/session authority security providers and observers shared infrastructure APIs (players, authorization, channels)
RESOURCE resources: gameplay modules (jobs, economy, housing, etc.) thin transport handlers domain services

sections.heading: How OpenCore Helps
sections.content:
Ports provide local/remote implementations transparently.
Same abstractions are used across modes.
Runtime setup enforces provider requirements in CORE.

sections.heading: Practical Rules
sections.content:
Keep cross-resource APIs stable and versioned.
Avoid direct global state coupling between resources.
Put shared contracts/types in dedicated shared modules.
Add explicit fallback behavior for temporary CORE unavailability.

sections.heading: Deployment Checklist
sections.content:
Define which resource owns each domain boundary.
Keep security and identity in CORE.
Load CORE before dependent RESOURCE modules.
Validate startup with integration smoke checks.

title: Session Recovery

sections.heading: What It Solves
sections.content: After resource restarts, players may remain connected while in-memory session maps are reset. Session recovery reconstructs missing runtime sessions safely.

sections.heading: Recovery Flow
sections.content:
SessionRecoveryService performs:
read connected player sources from runtime
check which players already have an active session
recreate missing sessions via lifecycle port binding
emit internal recovery event for downstream hooks

sections.heading: Current Behavior
sections.content:
Recovers basic identity/session structure.
Does not magically restore every domain state.
Designed for runtime continuity during restarts and development reloads.

sections.heading: Operational Guidance
sections.content:
Run recovery at startup for CORE resources.
Keep persistence and auth flows idempotent.
Treat recovered sessions as rehydrated runtime state, not full domain replay.

sections.heading: Observability
sections.content:
Track at least:
total connected players
recovered session count
already-existing session count
recovery errors/warnings

title: Appearance

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The server-side AppearanceService provides authoritative control over player appearance data. It works in conjunction with the Client Appearance API to ensure appearance changes are validated and synchronized.

sections.heading: Key Responsibilities
sections.content:
Persistence — Stores and retrieves appearance data from the player's session.
Validation — Ensures appearance data integrity before broadcasting to clients.
Synchronization — Coordinates appearance updates between server state and client rendering.

sections.heading: Usage
sections.content:
The server-side appearance API is typically used during:
Player session load (restoring saved appearance)
Character creation/selection flows
Admin commands that modify player appearance

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
For client-side rendering and direct ped manipulation, see the Client Appearance API.
Appearance data should be persisted via the PlayerPersistenceContract.

title: Channels

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The Channels API provides a pub/sub communication system for grouping players and broadcasting messages to specific audiences. Channels are ideal for proximity-based systems, team communication, or any scenario where you need to target a subset of connected players.

sections.heading: create()
sections.content: Creates a new channel with a unique identifier.

sections.heading: subscribe() / unsubscribe()
sections.content: Adds or removes a player from a channel.

sections.heading: broadcast()
sections.content: Sends a message to all players subscribed to a channel.

sections.heading: getSubscribers()
sections.content:
Returns all players currently subscribed to a channel.
--

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
Channels are server-side only. Clients receive messages via standard net events.
Channels are automatically cleaned up when all subscribers disconnect.

title: Chat

sections.heading: Description
sections.content:
Chat is the server runtime API for sending chat messages to players. It abstracts underlying network events and provides a clean API for broadcast, private, and proximity communication.
By using this service instead of raw emitNet calls, you ensure that messages follow the framework's standard formatting and color protocols.

sections.heading: broadcast()
sections.content:
Sends a message to every player currently connected to the server. message — The text content of the message.
author — (Optional) The name shown as the sender. Defaults to SYSTEM.
color — (Optional) An RGB object { r, g, b }. Defaults to white.

sections.heading: sendPrivate()
sections.content: Sends a message to a specific player.

sections.heading: sendNearby()
sections.content: Sends a message to all players within a certain distance of an origin player. Ideal for local roleplay chat.

sections.heading: clearChat() / clearChatAll()
sections.content: Clears the chat box for a specific player or for everyone on the server.

sections.heading: broadcastSystem()
sections.content:
A helper method to send important system-wide alerts with a distinct light blue color.
--

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
All messaging is performed via network events (core:chat:message, core:chat:addMessage).
Colors are passed as simple objects: { r: 255, g: 255, b: 255 }.

title: Appearance

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The client-side AppearanceService is the authority for managing ped aesthetics. It handles the complex process of applying head blends, face features, overlays (makeup, beard), clothing components, props, and tattoos.

sections.heading: Sequential Application
sections.content:
Applying appearance in GTA V requires a specific order to avoid glitches. The service handles this automatically:
HeadBlend — Essential foundation for face features and overlays.
Face Features — Bone-level facial adjustments.
Components — Clothing and hair.
Props — Hats, glasses, ears.
Head Overlays — Skin details and makeup.
Tattoos — Applied via decorations.

sections.heading: Validation
sections.content: Includes a validateAppearance method to ensure data integrity before applying it to the ped.

sections.heading: applyAppearance()
sections.content: Applies a full PlayerAppearance object to a ped handle.

sections.heading: getAppearance()
sections.content:
Reads the current clothing and props from a ped.
Note: HeadBlend and Overlay data cannot be read back from the engine and must be tracked via state.

sections.heading: getNumComponentDrawables() / getNumPropDrawables()
sections.content:
Retrieves the total number of available variations for a specific slot (e.g., how many jackets exist for this model).
--

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
HeadBlend must be set before FaceFeatures or HeadOverlays will work.
Tattoos are managed via addDecoration and require the collection and overlay hashes.
Use setDefaultAppearance() to reset a ped to its base state.
For server-side appearance persistence, see the Server Appearance API.

title: Blips

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The BlipService manages map icons (blips) in the GTA V world. It provides a managed system that tracks blips by ID, allowing for easy updates and cleanup.

sections.heading: create()
sections.content: Creates a blip at a specific world coordinate.

sections.heading: createForEntity()
sections.content: Attaches a blip to an entity (Ped, Vehicle, or Object). The blip will follow the entity as it moves.

sections.heading: createForRadius()
sections.content: Creates a circular area blip on the map.

sections.heading: update()
sections.content: Updates the options (color, scale, label, etc.) of an existing blip without removing it.

sections.heading: setRoute()
sections.content: Draws a GPS route from the player's current position to the specified blip.

sections.heading: remove() / removeAll()
sections.content:
Removes a specific blip or all managed blips.
--

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
All created blips are stored in an internal registry for mass cleanup via removeAll().
Common options include sprite (icon ID), color, scale, and shortRange.

title: Camera
description: Low-level scripted camera control for client-side gameplay and cinematic workflows.

sections.heading: Description
sections.content:
The Camera API is the low-level wrapper around FiveM scripted camera natives.
It gives you full control over camera lifecycle, transforms, interpolation, pointing, and shake.
Use this API when you need deterministic camera behavior for gameplay features, custom views, or cutscene tooling.

sections.heading: When to Use
sections.content:
Use Camera for direct and manual camera control.
Use Cinematic when you need a timeline-based sequence with shots, effects, and runtime control.

sections.heading: create()
sections.content: Creates a scripted camera and optionally applies the initial transform.

sections.heading: getActiveCam()
sections.content: Returns the currently tracked active camera handle.

sections.heading: setActive()
sections.content: Sets camera active state and updates internal tracking.

sections.heading: render() / isRendering()
sections.content: Enables or disables scripted camera rendering and checks current render status.

sections.heading: destroy() / destroyAll() / reset()
sections.content:
Lifecycle cleanup methods.
destroy removes one camera.
destroyAll removes all scripted cameras.
reset disables rendering (if enabled) and clears all managed cameras.

sections.heading: setPosition() / setRotation() / setFov() / setTransform()
sections.content: Applies camera transform values in world space.

sections.heading: pointAtCoords() / pointAtEntity() / stopPointing()
sections.content: Controls camera look-at behavior.

sections.heading: interpolate()
sections.content: Interpolates between two cameras using native interpolation.

sections.heading: shake() / stopShaking()
sections.content: Starts or stops camera shake effects.

sections.heading: Best Practices
sections.content:
Always cleanup (destroy/destroyAll/reset) when the sequence is done.
Avoid creating many cameras per frame; reuse handles when possible.
Keep interpolation durations consistent with your UX pacing.
Use setTransform when applying multiple transform values together.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
Camera is intentionally low-level and does not provide timeline orchestration.
setRotation defaults to rotation order 2 unless you override it.
render(false) should be called before leaving custom camera flow.

title: Cinematic
description: Timeline-based cinematic orchestration with shots, effects, and runtime controls.

sections.heading: Description
sections.content:
The Cinematic API is a high-level timeline system built on top of Camera.
It lets you define shot sequences, interpolation behavior, look targets, and camera effects,
then control playback through a runtime handle.

sections.heading: When to Use
sections.content:
Use Cinematic for intros, mission reveals, scripted moments, and camera tours.
Use Camera directly when you only need one-shot manual camera control.

sections.heading: scene()
sections.content: Creates a fluent SceneBuilder bound to this cinematic instance.

sections.heading: start()
sections.content: Starts a cinematic immediately and returns a mutable CinematicHandle.

sections.heading: play()
sections.content: Starts and awaits completion in one call.

sections.heading: isRunning() / cancel()
sections.content: Checks if there is an active timeline and cancels it.

sections.heading: registerEffect()
sections.content: Registers a custom reusable effect in the effect registry.

sections.heading: Runtime Handle (CinematicHandle)
sections.content: start() returns a CinematicHandle with mutable runtime controls and events.

sections.heading: Result and events
sections.content:
Available events:
shotStart
shotEnd
effectApplied
paused
resumed
completed
cancelled
interrupted

sections.heading: Pos
sections.content:
Position/node builders used in shots:
Pos.coords(x, y, z)
Pos.entity(entity, offset?)
Pos.entityBone(entity, bone, offset?)
Pos.anchor(name, offset?)
Pos.resolver(() =Vector3 Promise<Vector3)
Each returns a NodeBuilder with helpers like .offset(...), .rot(...), and .fov(...).

sections.heading: Fx
sections.content:
Effect builder helpers:
Fx.effect(id, params?)
Fx.fadeIn(ms?)
Fx.fadeOut(ms?)
Fx.camShake(type?, amplitude?)
Fx.timecycle(name?, strength?)
Fx.letterbox(top?, bottom?, alpha?)
Fx.subtitle(text, durationMs?)
Effects can be windowed using .from(ms), .to(ms), or .window(fromMs, toMs).

sections.heading: Best Practices
sections.content:
Use stable shot ids (id) if you need runtime patching with replaceShot.
Prefer scene().play(...) for simple linear flows and start(...) for advanced controls.
Keep shots focused; split long movements into multiple shots for better tuning.
Use presets/effects sparingly to avoid visual overload and maintain readability.
Validate anchors and effect ids early to avoid runtime validation errors.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
A new cinematic interrupts any currently running one.
Invalid scene definitions throw CinematicValidationError with detailed issues.
Built-in effect presets include dramaticintro, actionchase, and dialogscene.
On resource stop, active cinematics are cancelled and camera state is reset.

title: Markers

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The MarkerService handles the rendering of 3D markers (arrows, cylinders, circles) in the game world. It includes a managed system that handles the per-frame DrawMarker calls automatically through an internal tick.

sections.heading: create()
sections.content:
Registers a persistent marker that will be rendered every frame. Options include:
type — Marker ID (0-43).
scale — Vector3 size.
color — RGBA object.
bobUpAndDown — Vertical animation.
rotate — Continuous rotation.

sections.heading: remove() / removeAll()
sections.content: Stops rendering and deletes markers from the managed registry.

sections.heading: drawOnce()
sections.content:
Draws a marker for exactly one frame. Useful for logic already running inside a @OnTick().
--

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
The service automatically starts/stops its internal tick based on whether there are active markers, optimizing performance.
Markers created via create() are identified by a unique string ID.

title: Notifications

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The NotificationService provides a clean, high-level API for interacting with the native GTA V "Thefeed" system. It handles everything from simple text messages to advanced notifications with textures and icons.

sections.heading: show()
sections.content: Displays a standard native notification above the minimap.

sections.heading: showWithType()
sections.content: Shows a notification with a specific framework icon (info, success, warning, error).

sections.heading: showAdvanced()
sections.content: Displays a rich notification with a custom texture dictionary and icon.

sections.heading: showHelp() / showFloatingHelp()
sections.content:
showHelp — Displays text in the top-left corner (standard FiveM help text).
showFloatingHelp — Displays text directly above the player's head in the 3D world.

sections.heading: showSubtitle()
sections.content:
Displays a centered text message at the bottom of the screen, typically used for dialogue or mission instructions.
--

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
All text components are automatically handled by the service using AddTextComponentString.
Use clearHelp() and clearSubtitle() to stop showing persistent messages.

title: Peds

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The PedService provides tools for spawning and managing non-player characters (NPCs). It handles model loading, relationship groups, and complex tasks like animations or combat attributes.

sections.heading: spawn()
sections.content: Asynchronously loads a model and creates an NPC.

sections.heading: playAnimation()
sections.content: Loads an animation dictionary and plays it on a ped. Supports blending and flags.

sections.heading: getClosest() / getNearby()
sections.content: Search utilities to find peds in the player's vicinity.

sections.heading: lookAtEntity() / walkTo()
sections.content: High-level task wrappers for AI behavior.

sections.heading: deleteAll()
sections.content:
Batch deletion of all managed peds.
--

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
Managed peds are tracked by the service for easy batch deletion via deleteAll().
Use blockEvents: true to prevent NPCs from reacting to ambient game events (shots, crashes), which is standard for quest or shop NPCs.

title: Progress

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The ProgressService provides a visual indicator for timed actions (e.g., "Repairing Vehicle", "Searching Bin"). It handles the UI, player animations, and prop attachments in a single call.

sections.heading: start()
sections.content:
Starts a progress bar and waits for it to complete or be cancelled. Options include:
label — Text shown on the bar.
duration — Time in milliseconds.
animation — (Optional) Dict and Anim to play.
prop — (Optional) Model and Bone to attach.
disableMovement / disableCombat — Security flags to restrict player actions.
canCancel — Whether the player can cancel (e.g., by pressing ESC).
useCircular — Use a circular busy spinner instead of a linear bar.
--

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
Returns a Promise<boolean: true if the duration elapsed, false if the player cancelled.
Handles cleanup of animations and attached props automatically upon completion or cancellation.

title: Spawn

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The SpawnService manages the complete lifecycle of a player joining the server, from the initial connection to the final fade-in when the character is ready to play.

sections.heading: Robust Lifecycle Management
sections.content:
Spawning in FiveM is complex. The SpawnService handles:
Waiting for the network session to be ready.
Loading the player model.
Ensuring the physical ped exists.
Loading collisions at the spawn point (to prevent falling through the map).
Resurrecting the local player cleanly.

sections.heading: Fade Transitions
sections.content:
The service automatically handles DoScreenFadeOut and DoScreenFadeIn during the spawn process, ensuring a smooth transition for the player.
In FiveM, the spawn bridge also shuts down the loading screen by default as part of the initial spawn flow.

sections.heading: spawn()
sections.content:
Performs the initial spawn. Typically called once when the player first joins or selects a character. SpawnOptions supports:
appearance?: PlayerAppearance
skipLoadingScreenShutdown?: boolean

sections.heading: respawn()
sections.content: Used for resurrecting a dead player or moving them to a new location while maintaining their current model and state.

sections.heading: teleportTo()
sections.content: A safe teleportation method that ensures collisions are loaded at the destination before moving the ped.

sections.heading: waitUntilSpawned()
sections.content:
A helper that allows other services or controllers to pause execution until the player has successfully completed their first spawn.
--

sections.heading: FiveM manual loading screen control
sections.content: If your FiveM resource uses loadscreenmanualshutdown 'yes', you can keep the loading screen visible until your scene is ready:

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
Timeouts: Built-in timeouts for network, ped, and collision loading prevent the client from hanging indefinitely.
Appearance: If an appearance object is provided, it uses AppearanceService to apply clothing and facial features automatically during the spawn.
FiveM: skipLoadingScreenShutdown is primarily intended for FiveM cinematic intro and character selection flows. When set, your code becomes responsible for calling ShutdownLoadingScreenNui().

title: Streaming

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The StreamingService simplifies the process of requesting and loading game assets. In FiveM, assets like models and animations must be explicitly requested and loaded into memory before they can be used. This service provides a Promise-based API to handle this cleanly.

sections.heading: requestModel()
sections.content: Loads a Ped, Vehicle, or Object model into memory.

sections.heading: requestAnimDict()
sections.content: Loads an animation dictionary.

sections.heading: requestPtfxAsset()
sections.content: Loads a particle effect (PTFX) asset.

sections.heading: requestTextureDict()
sections.content: Loads a texture dictionary for UI or world draw calls.

sections.heading: startParticleEffect()
sections.content: A high-level helper that ensures the asset is loaded before starting a particle effect at a coordinate.

sections.heading: releaseModel() / releaseAnimDict() / releaseAll()
sections.content:
Frees loaded assets from memory.
--

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
Automatic Tracking: The service tracks all loaded assets.
Resource Cleanup: Call releaseAll() to free up memory.
Timeouts: All request methods include a default 10-second timeout to prevent infinite loops if an asset is missing.

title: TextUI

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The TextUIService handles rendering text both on the screen (2D) and attached to world coordinates (3D). It is ideal for interaction prompts or floating labels above objects.

sections.heading: show() / hide()
sections.content: Displays/hides a persistent text prompt at the bottom-right of the screen.

sections.heading: drawText3D()
sections.content: Renders text at a world coordinate. The service automatically calculates screen projection and applies distance-based scaling. --

sections.content:
drawText3D must be called every frame (inside a tick) to remain visible.
show() is persistent and managed by an internal service tick until hide() is called.
Scaling in 3D is automatically adjusted so the text remains readable as the camera moves.

title: Vehicle

sections.heading: Description
sections.content:
The client-side vehicle API consists of two layers:
VehicleClientService — High-level, server-synchronized operations (spawn, delete, mods).
VehicleService (Client) — Low-level, direct handle manipulation (repair, fuel, local mods).
--

sections.heading: VehicleClientService (Server-Synchronized)
sections.content: Methods like createVehicle and deleteVehicle don't execute locally — they send requests to the server and wait for a response, ensuring the server remains the source of truth.

sections.heading: createVehicle()
sections.content: Requests the server to spawn a vehicle. Returns a Promise with the result.

sections.heading: getClosestVehicle()
sections.content: Local helper to find the nearest vehicle handle.

sections.heading: getVehicleState()
sections.content: Reads custom metadata stored in the vehicle's State Bag.

sections.heading: repairVehicle() / setDoorsLocked()
sections.content: Sends requests to the server to modify the vehicle's condition or security.

sections.heading: VehicleService — Low-Level (Local)
sections.content: Provides direct interaction with vehicle handles for immediate operations.

sections.heading: spawn()
sections.content:
Directly calls CreateVehicle (Client).
Warning: Vehicles spawned this way are not managed by the server and may not synchronize correctly.

sections.heading: repair()
sections.content: Instantly fixes all damage, deformations, and engine health.

sections.heading: setFuel() / getFuel()
sections.content: Wrappers for managing vehicle fuel levels (0-100).

sections.heading: setMods()
sections.content: Applies a batch of modifications directly to a vehicle handle.

sections.heading: When to use which?
sections.content:
Need Use -- -- Spawn a vehicle that all players see VehicleClientService.createVehicle() Repair a vehicle you're sitting in VehicleService.repair() Read vehicle state bags VehicleClientService.getVehicleState() Set fuel locally VehicleService.setFuel() VehicleClientService works with Network IDs (synchronized).
VehicleService works with handles (local).

title: Parallel Compute

sections.heading: Description
sections.content:
ParallelCompute is OpenCore's runtime API for handling CPU-intensive tasks without blocking the main GTA/FiveM thread. It uses a Worker Pool to execute TypeScript code in background threads.
This is critical for maintaining high server FPS when performing heavy operations like complex pathfinding, data processing, or large-scale mathematical simulations.

sections.heading: Worker Pool
sections.content: The service manages a pool of background workers (Native Workers). When you submit a task, it is queued and picked up by the first available worker.

sections.heading: Task Execution
sections.content: Tasks must be defined in a way that they can be serialized and sent to a worker. The service handles the communication and returns a Promise that resolves when the worker completes the task.

sections.heading: run()
sections.content: Executes a task in a background worker.

sections.heading: getStats()
sections.content:
Returns information about the current state of the pool: active workers, pending tasks in queue, and completed task count.

sections.heading: Why use Parallelism?
sections.content:
FiveM runs the main script logic on a single thread. If you perform a calculation that takes 50ms, the entire server "freezes" for 50ms, causing lag and dropped frames.
By offloading that calculation:
The main thread stays free to process networking and game logic.
The calculation runs at full speed on a separate CPU core.
You receive the result via a Promise when it's ready.

sections.heading: Example Use Cases
sections.content:
Pathfinding — Calculating routes for complex AI.
JSON Processing — Parsing extremely large data structures.
Cryptography — Generating hashes or encrypted tokens.
Image/Data Compression — Processing assets on the fly.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
Isolation: Workers do not have access to the global scope of your resource. You must pass all required data via the task arguments.
Natives: FiveM Natives are generally not available inside worker threads. Parallelism is for pure TypeScript/JavaScript logic.
Overhead: Moving data between threads has a small cost. Only use this service for tasks that take significant time (1ms).

title: Vehicle Modifications

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The VehicleModificationService handles all visual and performance upgrades for vehicles. It is designed with Security First principles, ensuring that every modification is validated on the server before being broadcast to clients.

sections.heading: Ownership Validation
sections.content: Before applying any mod, the service verifies that the requesting player actually owns the vehicle or has "shared" access.

sections.heading: Proximity Checks
sections.content: The service ensures the player is within range (default 15.0 units) of the vehicle. This prevents "remote tuning" exploits.

sections.heading: Value Constraints
sections.content: All modification IDs (spoilers, engines, etc.) are clamped to valid ranges (-1 to 50) to prevent engine crashes or invalid state synchronization.

sections.heading: applyModifications()
sections.content: The primary method for batch-applying changes.

sections.heading: setColors()
sections.content: Updates primary and secondary colors using standard GTA color IDs.

sections.heading: setNeon()
sections.content: Configures neon light states (Left, Right, Front, Back) and their RGB color.

sections.heading: resetModifications()
sections.content:
Reverts a vehicle to its factory default state (removes all mods, resets colors to white/black).
--

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
Modifications are synchronized using the opencore:vehicle:modified network event.
The service uses State Bags internally via the Vehicle entity to ensure persistence across sessions if the vehicle is saved.
windowTint, livery, and plateStyle are also managed here.

title: Vehicles

sections.heading: Description
sections.content:
Vehicles is the server-side API for authoritative vehicle management in OpenCore.
It centralizes server-side spawning, registry/index operations, ownership/proximity checks, cleanup, and serialization.

sections.heading: Server-Authoritative Spawning
sections.content: Unlike standard FiveM scripts that spawn vehicles on the client, OpenCore uses CreateVehicleServerSetter. The server creates the entity directly, ensuring it exists even if the creating player crashes or leaves.

sections.content: Spawns a vehicle on the server with specific options.

sections.heading: createForPlayer()
sections.content: Spawns a vehicle and assigns player ownership automatically. On success, emits a warp event to place the player in driver seat.

title: CLI Overview

sections.heading: What is OpenCore CLI?
sections.content:
The OpenCore CLI is the official command-line tool used to build, validate, and orchestrate OpenCore-based projects.
It is not a generic TypeScript compiler. It understands FiveM, RageMP, and RedM runtimes, OpenCore architecture, and the constraints of each execution environment.
Conceptually, it plays a role similar to:
NestJS CLI (project orchestration)
Vite (fast, opinionated builds)
…but designed specifically for FiveM, RageMP, RedM, and OpenCore.
--

sections.heading: What problem does it solve?
sections.content:
FiveM, RageMP, and RedM are not a single runtime.
You are dealing with:
Node.js (server)
Neutral JS runtimes (client)
Browsers (NUI / Views)
Each with different rules, APIs, and limitations.
The OpenCore CLI:
Detects what you are building
Validates what is allowed
Produces runtime-safe artifacts
Fails early when something is invalid
This removes an entire class of hard-to-debug runtime errors.
--

sections.heading: Core concepts
sections.content: The CLI understands three types of components:

sections.heading: 🧠 Core
sections.content:
The central brain of your server.
Hosts the OpenCore runtime
Exposes exports to other resources
Owns global systems (commands, players, identity)
There is usually one Core per server.
--

sections.heading: 🛰️ Satellite Resources
sections.content:
Modular resources that depend on the Core.
Contain gameplay logic
Register commands and events
Delegate shared systems to Core
Built for small bundles and fast iteration
This is the recommended way to scale a server.
--

sections.heading: 📦 Standalone Resources
sections.content:
Independent resources that do not rely on OpenCore.
Legacy Lua scripts
Utility JS resources
Third-party tools
The CLI supports them, but does not enforce framework rules.
--

sections.heading: High-level build flow
sections.content:
`
You do not configure this manually. The CLI infers it from structure and intent.
--

sections.heading: Why Go?
sections.content:
The CLI and compiler are written in Go (Golang) by design.
Key reasons:
Performance: Parallel builds using goroutines
Single binary: No Node.js dependency for the tool itself
Low memory usage: Stable even with many resources
Fast startup: Near-instant command execution
This makes the CLI reliable in both development and CI environments.
--

sections.heading: CLI syntax basics
sections.content:
Command arguments follow a simple convention:
<argument→ required [argument] → optional Example: `
This mirrors standard CLI conventions and avoids ambiguity.
--

sections.heading: Automatic discovery
sections.content:
The CLI performs automatic project analysis: Detects server entrypoints: main.ts, index.ts, server.ts Detects client entrypoints: client.ts, index.ts Discovers NUI / view entrypoints Infers runtime targets per file
No explicit configuration is required.
--

sections.heading: Package manager: pnpm (recommended)
sections.content:
While npm and yarn are supported, pnpm is strongly recommended.
Reasons: Faster installs Lower disk usage Strict dependency isolation Optimized integration with the CLI linker
The CLI is designed around pnpm’s dependency model.
--

sections.heading: NUI / Views support
sections.content:
OpenCore treats views as browser builds handled by Vite or a minimal vanilla fallback.
Supported modes: Vite → recommended for React, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Tailwind, PostCSS, Sass, and other modern UI stacks Vanilla → simple HTML/CSS/JS/TS pages compiled directly by the CLI
The CLI also exposes createOpenCoreViteConfig from @open-core/cli/vite so project-level Vite configs can stay small and consistent.
If required dependencies are missing or a legacy framework mode is used: The build fails A clea

sections.heading: Runtime Adapters
sections.content:
An Adapter defines the target platform for your project. It controls the build pipeline, output structure, and platform-specific behavior.
OpenCore supports multiple platforms through official adapters: Adapter Status Use Case FiveM Stable FiveM server builds RageMP Stable Rage Multiplayer builds RedM Coming Soon RedM-specific runtime path under the same adapter model Node Default Local development / testing

sections.heading: Defining an Adapter
sections.content:
Configure your adapter in opencore.config.ts: The adapter is the central runtime switch. It determines:
Build targets and output layout
Manifest generation
Platform-specific optimizations
Runtime behavior

sections.heading: Project Initialization
sections.content:
When creating a new project, specify the adapter with --adapter:
```bash

sections.heading: Interactive wizard
sections.content: opencore init my-server

sections.heading: Non-interactive with platform
sections.content:
opencore init my-server --adapter=fivem
opencore init my-server --adapter=ragemp

sections.heading: No adapter (uses framework default - Node)
sections.content:
opencore init my-server --adapter=none
```

sections.heading: Validation
sections.content:
The CLI validates your adapter configuration automatically. Use opencore doctor to verify your setup is correct and all dependencies are properly installed.
--

sections.heading: Philosophy
sections.content:
The OpenCore CLI is opinionated by design.
Its goals are: Safety over flexibility Correctness over convenience Explicit failures instead of silent bugs
You can build your own tooling —
but the CLI is the reference implementation for OpenCore projects.
--

The following sections explain how to use it.

title: Client Runtime Overview

sections.heading: What is the Client Runtime?
sections.content: The Client Runtime is the player-facing layer of OpenCore. It handles interaction with the GTA V engine, UI management, and local entity control. Unlike the server which handles global authority, the client focuses on responsiveness, visuals, and local player interaction.

sections.heading: Automatic Injection
sections.content: Just like on the server, OpenCore handles the lifecycle of client services automatically. Use @Controller() to define entry points and @Service() for reusable client business logic. Key rule: Never use new MyService(). Define the service in your constructor to receive the framework-managed instance.

sections.heading: Core Responsibilities
sections.content:
The client runtime handles several critical areas:
Streaming — Loading and unloading models, animations, and textures.
Visuals — Managing blips, markers, and native notifications.
Life Cycle — Handling the complex process of spawning and resurrecting the player.
Interactions — Displaying progress bars and managing WebView communication.
Input — Binding keyboard keys and game events to controller methods.

sections.heading: Available Client APIs
sections.content: API Responsibility -- -- Spawn Orchestrates the complete player spawn/respawn lifecycle. Appearance Manages ped aesthetics (clothing, face, tattoos). Notifications Displays native GTA V notifications, help text, and subtitles. Blips Manages map icons for entities, positions, and radii. Markers Renders 3D markers in the game world. Peds Spawns and manages NPCs with animations and AI tasks. TextUI Renders 2D/3D text prompts and labels. Streaming High-level API for requesting and releasing game ass

sections.heading: Design Notes
sections.content:
Client controllers are event-driven, not request-driven.
Prefer @Interval() over @OnTick() when possible to reduce CPU usage.
@LocalEvent() is the recommended way to communicate between client systems.
WebView communication is explicit and isolated through @OnView().

title: WebView Bridge

sections.heading: Description
sections.content:
The WebView Bridge is the communication layer between your client-side gameplay logic and your web-based UI (HTML/CSS/JavaScript).
OpenCore provides:
WebViewBridge class for programmatic UI control
@OnView() decorator for handling UI messages
WebViewService for advanced use cases

sections.heading: WebViewBridge

title: Binary Protocol
description: Low-level communication protocol between OpenCore and external binary processes.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Binary Protocol defines how OpenCore communicates with external native processes
(C++, Rust, Go, Java, etc.) in a deterministic, language-agnostic, and runtime-safe way.
This protocol is the foundation of:
@BinaryService
@BinaryCall
@BinaryEvent
It is intentionally simple, explicit, and stream-based, avoiding RPC frameworks,
shared memory, or FFI bindings.
At its core, the protocol is:
Transport: stdin / stdout
Encoding: UTF-8
Format: JSON (one message per line)
Direction: Bidirectional
Mode

sections.heading: Transport Model
sections.content:
Each binary is spawned as a child process.
Communication happens exclusively through:
stdin → messages sent from OpenCore to the binary
stdout → messages sent from the binary to OpenCore
stderr → logs, diagnostics, crashes (not part of the protocol)
Each message must be a single JSON object terminated by \n. Multi-line JSON or pretty printing is not allowed.
--

sections.heading: Message Categories
sections.content:
There are three message categories:
Requests (OpenCore → Binary)
Responses (Binary → OpenCore)
Events (Binary → OpenCore)
Each category has a strict schema.
--

sections.content: Requests are sent when using @BinaryCall.

sections.heading: Responses (Binary → OpenCore)

sections.heading: Events (Binary → OpenCore)
sections.content:
Events are unsolicited messages emitted by the binary.
They are handled by @BinaryEvent.

sections.heading: Fields
sections.content: Field Type Required type "event" yes event string yes data any no

sections.heading: Example
sections.content:
Events do not receive responses.
--

sections.heading: Message Ordering Guarantees
sections.content:
Messages are processed in arrival order Responses are matched using id Events are handled independently from request lifecycle
There is no guarantee that events will arrive before or after a response unless
explicitly designed by the binary.
--

sections.heading: Invalid JSON
sections.content: If the binary writes invalid JSON: The line is discarded The error is logged The process may be terminated depending on severity

sections.heading: Unknown id
sections.content: If a response references an unknown id: The response is ignored A warning is logged

sections.heading: Missing Response
sections.content:
If a response is not received within the configured timeout: The call fails The promise is rejected The binary process may be restarted
--

sections.heading: Design Constraints (Intentional)
sections.content:
The protocol deliberately does not support: Streaming responses Partial results Shared state between calls Binary payloads Auto-retries at protocol level
These decisions keep the protocol: Debuggable with echo Implementable in <50 lines in most languages Safe under crashes Predictable under load

Each decorator builds on this protocol without extending it.
--

sections.heading: Summary
sections.content:
The Binary Protocol is: Minimal Explicit Deterministic Language-neutral
If you can read JSON from stdin and write JSON to stdout, you can integrate with OpenCore.
Nothing more is required.

title: Events API
description: Core event bus used by OpenCore for all event-based communication.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Events API is the central event dispatch system in OpenCore.
It provides a unified, platform-agnostic way to:
Emit events
Subscribe to events
Dispatch events across different execution contexts
All event-based communication in OpenCore — including network events, framework events,
runtime events, and local events — ultimately flows through the Events API.
--

sections.heading: EventsAPI as the Core Event Bus
Injection and Usage
sections.content:
The Events API is available through dependency injection.
It can be injected into services, controllers, or any injectable class. Key properties: No platform imports No global functions Same API on server and client Transport resolved automatically The side, server or client`, must be defined for correct typing.
--

sections.heading: events.emit(...)
sections.content:
Emits an event into the OpenCore event system. Example: What happens internally depends on context: The active transport determines how the event propagates The EventsAPI dispatches the event to all matching handlers Registered decorators and runtime listeners receive it
The caller does not need to know how the event is delivered.
--

sections.heading: events.on(...)
sections.content:
Registers a runtime event listener. Example: Characteristics: Subscriptions are dynamic Handlers are executed through the same event bus as decorators Errors inside handlers are isolated and logged
--

sections.heading: Relation to Decorators
sections.content:
Decorators are not separate systems.
They are declarative ways to register handlers that are later attached
to the EventsAPI.

sections.heading: Conceptual Flow
sections.content:
Decorator stores metadata
Framework bootstraps the resource
Metadata is resolved
Handlers are registered into the EventsAPI
Events are dispatched through the same bus
From the point of view of execution, there is no difference between: A handler registered via a decorator A handler registered via events.on(...)
Both are dispatched identically.
--

sections.heading: Event Scopes
sections.content:
The Events API does not expose transport or scope details directly.
Instead, it operates on logical events.
Depending on context and configuration, an event may represent: A network-level event A framework lifecycle event A runtime or resource-level event A local in-process event
The distinction is resolved internally.
--

sections.heading: Error Handling
sections.content:
The Events API follows strict safety rules: Emitting an event never throws Handler errors are caught and logged One failing handler does not affect others Events never block execution flow
This ensures stability even under faulty handlers.
--

sections.heading: When to Use the Events API
sections.content:
Use the Events API when: Emitting events from services or domain logic Building reusable, platform-agnostic modules Needing dynamic subscriptions Interacting with the core event bus directly
Use decorators when: Declaring static handlers Binding to lifecycle or communication entry points Structuring controller interfaces
They are complementary, not exclusive.
--

sections.heading: Design Principles
sections.content:
The Events API is designed around: A single source of truth for events Clear separation between declaration and execution Strong isolation and error containment Platform independence
This makes the system predictable, extensible, and easy to reason about.
--

sections.heading: Summary
sections.content:
The Events API is the heart of OpenCore’s event system.
It provides: A unified event bus Platform-agnostic communication A foundation for all event decorators Safe and deterministic dispatch
Understanding the Events API means understanding how events work in OpenCore.

title: Communication Overview

sections.heading: Core Communication Primitives
sections.content:
OpenCore provides three primary communication primitives:
Events
RPC (Remote Procedure Calls)
Binary Communication
Each one serves a different purpose and has distinct guarantees.
--

sections.heading: Events
sections.content:
Events are used to notify other parts of the system that something happened.
Characteristics:
Fire-and-forget
No response expected
No delivery guarantee
Low coupling
Events are ideal for:
State updates
Notifications
UI updates
Reactive behavior
Events exist at multiple levels:
Network events (server ↔ client)
Framework events (internal lifecycle)
Runtime events (platform-level)
Local events (in-process)
--

sections.heading: RPC (Remote Procedure Calls)
sections.content:
RPC is used when one side needs to ask the other side to execute logic and return a result.
Characteristics:
Request–response model
Correlated calls
Promise-based
Timeout and error handling
RPC is ideal for:
Queries
Commands that require confirmation
Client ↔ server interactions with results
RPC is directional and context-aware:
Clients usually call server logic
Servers may call client logic when necessary
--

sections.heading: Binary Communication
sections.content:
Binary communication allows OpenCore to interact with external native processes
written in languages such as C++, Rust, Go, or Java.
Characteristics:
Process isolation
stdin/stdout JSON protocol
Strong failure boundaries
Language-agnostic
This is used for:
CPU-intensive tasks
Native integrations
Security-sensitive operations
Performance-critical logic
--

sections.heading: Platform-Agnostic by Design
sections.content:
OpenCore separates communication intent from platform implementation.
User code interacts with:
EventsAPI
RpcAPI
These APIs are:
Injected via constructor
Independent of FiveM or any other platform
Resolved at runtime through adapters
FiveM is just one possible transport implementation.
--

sections.heading: APIs vs Decorators
sections.content: OpenCore intentionally distinguishes between:

sections.heading: APIs (Imperative)
sections.content:
Used to emit or invoke communication.
Examples:
events.emit(...)
rpc.call(...)
rpc.notify(...)
These are typically used inside services and controllers.
--

sections.heading: Decorators (Declarative)
Execution Contexts
sections.content:
Communication behaves differently depending on context: Context Can Emit Can Handle Server Events, RPC, Binaries Events, RPC Client Events, RPC Events, RPC Binary Events, RPC Calls only The framework resolves the correct behavior automatically.
--

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Tool
sections.content:
A simple rule of thumb:
Need to notify? → Use Events
Need a result? → Use RPC
Need native performance or isolation? → Use Binaries
Avoid overloading one mechanism to behave like another.
--

sections.heading: Design Philosophy
sections.content:
The communication system prioritizes:
Explicitness over magic
Determinism over convenience
Isolation over shared state
Clear failure modes
This makes systems easier to reason about, debug, and evolve.
--

sections.heading: Summary
sections.content:
OpenCore communication is:
Layered
Explicit
Platform-agnostic
Safe by default
Understanding these primitives is key to building reliable systems
on top of the framework.
The following sections dive deeper into each mechanism.

title: RPC API
description: Core request–response communication API in OpenCore.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The RPC API provides a platform-agnostic request–response communication system
in OpenCore.
It allows one execution context to invoke logic in another context and optionally
receive a result, with:
Correlation
Timeouts
Structured error handling
All RPC-based communication in OpenCore flows through the RpcAPI.
--

sections.heading: RpcAPI as the Core RPC Layer
sections.content:
The RpcAPI is the central execution layer for all RPC interactions.
All RPC decorators, including:
@OnRPC
@OnRPC
ultimately register their handlers into the RpcAPI during the bootstrap phase.
This means:
There is a single RPC dispatch mechanism
Decorators only declare handlers
Invocation, correlation, and resolution are handled centrally
All RPC calls in OpenCore are executed through the RpcAPI.
--

sections.heading: Injection and Usage
sections.content:
The RpcAPI is accessed through dependency injection.
It can be injected into services, controllers, or any injectable class. `
Key properties: No platform-specific imports Same API on server and client Context-aware behavior Transport resolved automatically
--

sections.heading: RPC Interaction Types
sections.content: The RpcAPI supports two interaction modes:

sections.heading: Call
sections.content:
A call expects a response. Characteristics: Returns a Promise<T Correlated with a unique request id Subject to timeout Resolves or rejects exactly once
Example: --

sections.heading: Notify
sections.content:
A notify sends a request without expecting a response. Characteristics: Fire-and-forget No promise No timeout No result tracking
Example: --

sections.heading: Parameters and Payloads
sections.content:
RPC payloads must be JSON-serializable. Validation is handled by the registered RPC handler, not by the API itself.
--

sections.heading: Targets and Context
sections.content: The RpcAPI is context-aware.

sections.heading: Client Context
sections.content: Target is implicit Calls are directed to the server target parameter is ignored --

sections.heading: Server Context
sections.content:
Target must be explicit or resolvable Calls can be directed to: A specific client Multiple clients All clients Target resolution is handled internally.
--

sections.heading: Timeouts
sections.content:
Every RPC call is executed with a timeout.
If the timeout expires: The call is rejected Pending state is cleaned up Late responses are discarded
Timeouts protect the runtime from stalled calls.
--

sections.heading: Error Handling
sections.content:
Errors can originate from: The remote handler throwing Validation failures Transport failures Timeouts
When an error occurs: The call promise is rejected Structured error information is propagated The runtime remains stable
Errors are isolated per call.
--

sections.heading: Relation to Decorators
sections.content: Decorators are declarative registration tools.

sections.heading: Conceptual Flow
sections.content:
Decorator stores metadata
Framework bootstraps the resource
RPC handlers are registered into the RpcAPI
Incoming calls are dispatched through the same API
Responses are correlated and returned
From an execution perspective, there is no distinction between
handlers registered via decorators or other means.
--

sections.heading: RPC vs Events
sections.content:
Aspect RPC API Events API Response Optional None Correlation Yes No Timeout Yes No Typical use Queries, commands Notifications Failure handling Explicit Best-effort Use the mechanism that matches your intent.
--

sections.heading: Design Principles
sections.content:
The RpcAPI is designed around: Explicit request–response semantics Deterministic behavior Clear failure modes Strong isolation between calls
This avoids ambiguity and hidden side effects.
--

sections.heading: Summary
sections.content:
The RpcAPI provides: A unified RPC execution layer Platform-agnostic invocation Call and notify semantics Built-in timeout and error handling
It is the foundation of all RPC communication in OpenCore.

title: RPC Overview
description: Remote Procedure Calls between server and client in OpenCore.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The RPC system in OpenCore provides a structured request–response communication model
between server and client.
RPC is used when one side needs to:
Invoke logic on the other side
Receive a response
Handle errors deterministically
Apply timeouts and correlation
Unlike network events, RPC calls are directional, correlated, and explicit.
--

sections.heading: What RPC Is (and Is Not)
sections.content:
RPC in OpenCore is:
A request–response mechanism
Asynchronous and promise-based
Built on top of FiveM network events
Explicit about targets and direction
RPC is not:
A broadcast system
A fire-and-forget mechanism
A streaming protocol
A replacement for authoritative server logic
If you need a value back, use RPC. If you only need to notify, use network events.
--

sections.heading: Communication Direction
sections.content: RPC is bidirectional, but the meaning of direction depends on context.

sections.heading: Server Context
sections.content:
From the server, RPC is typically used to:
Call logic on a specific client
Call logic on multiple clients (fan-out)
Notify clients without waiting for a result

sections.heading: Client Context
sections.content:
From the client, RPC is typically used to:
Call authoritative server logic
Request validation or data
Trigger server-side actions
The framework automatically resolves context (server vs client) at runtime.
--

sections.heading: Call vs Notify
sections.content: RPC supports two interaction types:

sections.heading: Call
sections.content:
Expects a response
Returns a Promise<TUses request–response correlation
Subject to timeout

sections.heading: Notify
sections.content:
Does not expect a response
Fire-and-forget
No promise resolution
No timeout tracking
Both use the same transport layer.
--

sections.heading: Targets
sections.content:
RPC calls can be targeted.
On the server:
A specific player
Multiple players
All players
On the client:
The server (implicit)
Target resolution is handled by the transport adapter.
--

sections.heading: Message Flow (High-Level)
sections.content:
Caller sends an RPC request
Request is assigned a unique id
Target receives the request
Registered handler executes
Response (or error) is sent back
Pending promise is resolved or rejected
This flow is enforced by the framework.
--

sections.heading: Error Model
sections.content:
RPC errors are explicit.
Errors can originate from:
The handler throwing
Validation failures
Timeouts
Transport-level issues
When an error occurs:
The response is marked as failed
The promise is rejected
The caller receives structured error information
Errors never crash the runtime.
--

sections.heading: Timeouts
sections.content:
Every RPC call is executed with a timeout.
If no response is received:
The call fails
The pending promise is rejected
The handler result is discarded if it arrives late
Timeouts prevent:
Stalled gameplay logic
Memory leaks
Zombie promises
--

sections.heading: RPC vs Network Events
sections.content:
Aspect RPC Network Events Response Required (call) None Correlation Yes No Timeout Yes No Direction Explicit Broadcast-like Use case Queries, actions Notifications A common rule:
If you expect a result, use RPC. If you expect a reaction, use events.
--

sections.heading: Relation to Decorators
Design Philosophy
sections.content:
The RPC system prioritizes:
Explicitness over convenience
Determinism over magic
Safety over performance shortcuts
It is intentionally stricter than raw FiveM events.
--

sections.heading: Summary
sections.content:
RPC in OpenCore provides:
Deterministic request–response communication
Clear separation between notify and call
Built-in timeout and error handling
A stable foundation for client–server logic
If your logic needs answers, RPC is the correct tool.

content:
Overview
The RPC system in OpenCore provides a structured request–response communication model
between server and client.
RPC is used when one side needs to:
Invoke logic on the other side
Receive a response
Handle errors deterministically
Apply timeouts and correlation
Unlike network events, RPC calls are directional, correlated, and explicit.
--
What RPC Is (and Is Not)
RPC in OpenCore is:
A request–response mechanism
Asynchronous and promise-based
Built on top of FiveM network events
Explicit about targets and direction
RPC is not:
A broadcast system
A fire-and-forget mechanism
A streaming protocol
A replacement for authoritative server logic
If you need a value back, use RPC. If you only need to notify, use network events.
--
Communication Direction
RPC is bidirectional, but the meaning of direction depends on context.
Server Context
From the server, RPC is typically used to:
Call logic on a specific client
Call logic on multiple clients (fan-out)
Notify clients without waiting for a result
Client Context
From the client, RPC is typically used to:
Call authoritative server logic
Request validation or data
Trigger server-side actions
The framework automatically resolves context (server vs client) at runtime.
--
Core Concepts
Call vs Notify
RPC supports two interaction types:
Call
Expects a response
Returns a Promise<TUses request–response correlation
Subject to timeout
Notify
Does not expect a response
Fire-and-forget
No promise resolution
No timeout tracking
Both use the same transport layer.
--
Targets
RPC calls can be targeted.
On the server:
A specific player
Multiple players
All players
On the client:
The server (implicit)
Target resolution is handled by the transport adapter.
--
Message Flow (High-Level)
Caller sends an RPC request
Request is assigned a unique id
Target receives the request
Registered handler executes
Response (or error) is sent back
Pending promise is resolved or rejected
This flow is enforced by the framework.
--
Error Model
RPC errors are explicit.
Errors can originate from:
The handler throwing
Validation failures
Timeouts
Transport-level issues
When an error occurs:
The response is marked as failed
The promise is rejected
The caller receives structured error information
Errors never crash the runtime.
--
Timeouts
Every RPC call is executed with a timeout.
If no response is received:
The call fails
The pending promise is rejected
The handler result is discarded if it arrives late
Timeouts prevent:
Stalled gameplay logic
Memory leaks
Zombie promises
--
RPC vs Network Events Aspect RPC Network Events Response Required (call) None Correlation Yes No Timeout Yes No Direction Explicit Broadcast-like Use case Queries, actions Notifications A common rule:
If you expect a result, use RPC. If you expect a reaction, use events.
--
Relation to Decorators
This overview describes the transport and execution model.
The following decorators build on top of it:
@OnRPC() – server-side RPC handlers
@OnRPC() – client-side RPC handlers

title: The Compiler

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The OpenCore Compiler is the technical core of the OpenCore CLI. It is not just a transpiler or a bundler: it is a monorepo-aware build orchestrator designed for FiveM, RageMP, RedM, and similar GTA runtimes.
Its job is to:
Understand what each environment can and cannot do
Compile server, client, and UI (NUI) code correctly
Coordinate multiple resources in parallel
Produce drop-in ready artifacts for the selected adapter/runtime
All of this is done with performance, safety, and predictability a

sections.heading: The Compiler as a Monorepo Orchestrator 🧠
sections.content:
An OpenCore project is effectively a monorepo of runtime units: The compiler:
Discovers all resources automatically
Detects entrypoints per environment
Builds each unit independently
Runs them in parallel when possible
Resolves cross-resource framework contracts (CORE ↔ RESOURCE)
Think of it less as “tsc` for FiveM” and more as:
A coordinator that understands the topology of your server
--

sections.heading: Runtime Environments
sections.content:
OpenCore projects run JavaScript in three different environments.
The compiler enforces hard boundaries between them and adapts output to the selected runtime.

sections.heading: Runtime Matrix
sections.content: Environment Target Purpose What you can use What will break Server Node.js Backend logic Node APIs, DBs, filesystem DOM, Web APIs, GTA natives Client Neutral JS Gameplay logic GTA natives, runtime events Node APIs, browser APIs Views (NUI) Browser UI / HUD DOM, fetch, UI frameworks Node APIs, native APIs --

sections.heading: Server Environment (Node.js)
sections.content:
The server runs on the runtime provided by the selected adapter.
FiveM/RedM default to the standard resource layout used by those runtimes.
RageMP typically targets Node 14 and uses a split layout with packages/ and clientpackages/.
Build targets are selected by adapter defaults and can be overridden in config.

sections.heading: Intended responsibilities
sections.content:
Authentication & persistence
Command handling
Business logic
External APIs
Background jobs

sections.heading: Examples
sections.content:
✅ Allowed ❌ Forbidden The compiler: Targets Node explicitly Keeps nodemodules` when the adapter expects runtime resolution Preserves Node globals
--

sections.heading: Client Environment (Neutral JS / V8)
sections.content:
Client code runs inside the game client, not Node and not a browser.
This environment is intentionally minimal.

sections.heading: Intended responsibilities
sections.content: Player input Game state Entity interaction Natives and events

sections.heading: Examples
sections.content:
✅ Allowed ❌ Forbidden The compiler: Bundles everything into a single file Strips Node & browser globals Fails fast on incompatible imports
This is one of the main reasons a generic bundler is not enough.
--

sections.heading: Views (NUI / Browser)
sections.content:
Views run in an embedded Chromium instance.
This is browser-like, but not guaranteed to be modern Chrome.
RageMP CEF is especially old, so build targets and CSS processing matter more than in a normal web app.

sections.heading: Intended responsibilities
sections.content: UI / HUD Menus Web-based interactions Styling & animations

sections.heading: Examples
sections.content:
✅ Allowed ❌ Forbidden The compiler: Resolves views as either vite or vanilla Lets Vite own modern framework integration and CSS tooling Auto-resolves project-root PostCSS when present Builds optimized browser bundles and copies static assets (HTML, CSS, fonts, images)
If a project needs React, Vue, Svelte, Astro, or similar tooling, configure it in Vite rather than in the CLI.
Shared Vite configs should use @open-core/cli/vite so the CLI can resolve the view root, output directory, and PostCSS a

sections.heading: Automatic Environment Discovery 🔍
sections.content:
The compiler does zero-config discovery.
It scans for: server.ts, client.ts, index.ts, main.ts View entrypoints (views/, ui/, nui/) Shared root vite.config. or local view vite.config. Resource boundaries Binary files (bin/, bin/win32, bin/linux)
Diagram: If an environment does not exist, it is simply skipped.
--

sections.heading: Adapter-Aware Output Layout
sections.content:
The output layout depends on the selected adapter: FiveM/RedM: standard resource folders with fxmanifest.lua RageMP: split output into packages/ and clientpackages/
The compiler follows adapter metadata instead of forcing one fixed folder structure.
--

sections.heading: Technology Stack
sections.content:
The compiler is a hybrid system, each tool doing exactly what it’s best at: Go → orchestration, parallelism, filesystem, process control SWC (Rust) → TypeScript, decorators, metadata reflection esbuild → ultra-fast bundling and linking Custom plugins → adapter-specific runtime constraints and compatibility rules
This separation is deliberate: Go handles scale (esbuild and CLI) Rust handles syntax & speed (SWC) JS tooling handles ecosystem compatibility (embedded JS)
--

sections.heading: Parallel Build Model ⚡
sections.content:
Traditional builds are sequential.
OpenCore is not. Each resource: Is built in isolation Has its own dependency graph Does not block others
Typical results: 8–12 resources → < 1 second build CPU-bound, not IO-bound
--

sections.heading: Why this Matters
sections.content:
The compiler guarantees that: Server code cannot accidentally leak into client Client code cannot rely on Node UI code stays browser-safe CORE and RESOURCE builds stay contract-correct Large projects remain maintainable and fast
For UI projects, the preferred entry point is the shared helper exported by @open-core/cli/vite.
In short:
The compiler encodes the rules of the selected runtime so you don’t have to remember them.
--

sections.heading: Final Mental Model
sections.content: This is what enables OpenCore to scale from: a single script to a full modular server architecture 🚀
