title: Library API Usage
description: How to use OpenCore library runtime APIs and library events.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Library API provides a consistent runtime contract for domain libraries such as characters, inventory, and factions.
It gives each library:
A local event bus (on, once, off, emit)
A stable event naming model (buildEventName, buildLibraryEventId)
Runtime-side helpers (getLogger, getConfig)
Directional transport bridge methods (server/client)
This page focuses on usage of the API once a library instance already exists in your module.
For install-time extension and bootstrap registration, see P

sections.heading: 1) Local Domain Events
sections.content:
Every library exposes an in-memory event bus:
on(eventName, handler)
once(eventName, handler)
off(eventName, handler)
emit(eventName, payload?)
These are the events observed by @OnLibraryEvent(...).

sections.heading: 2) Event Naming
sections.content:
Libraries expose two naming helpers:
buildEventName(eventName) External namespaced format: opencore:<library:<eventbuildLibraryEventId(libraryName, eventName) Canonical domain id: <library:<event

sections.heading: 3) Runtime Metadata for Observers
sections.content:
When listening with @OnLibraryEvent(...), handlers receive metadata describing the origin:
libraryName
eventName
eventId
namespace
side

sections.heading: Server Library Runtime Methods
sections.content:
In addition to the base API, server libraries include:
emitExternal(eventName, payload?) Emits a server-side cross-resource event.
emitNetExternal(eventName, target, payload?) Emits a net event to a specific target.
getLogger() Namespaced logger for the library.
getConfig<T() Namespaced config accessor.

sections.heading: Client Library Runtime Methods
sections.content:
Client libraries include:
emitServer(eventName, payload?) Sends namespaced event to server.
getLogger() Client logger for the library.
getConfig<T() Namespaced config accessor.

sections.heading: OnLibraryEvent Scope
sections.content:
@OnLibraryEvent(...) and @OnLibraryEvent(...) observe only domain emissions from library.emit(...).
They do not observe transport bridge methods:
emitExternal(...)
emitNetExternal(...)
emitServer(...)
This keeps domain events and transport concerns clearly separated.

sections.heading: Practical Recommendations
sections.content:
Use emit(...) for domain-level signals (session:created, items:updated, faction:member-added).
Use OnLibraryEvent for optional listeners (projections, analytics, notifications).
Use bridge methods only when crossing runtime/resource boundaries is required.
Keep event names stable and explicit; treat them as part of your library contract.

sections.heading: When to Combine With Plugin API
sections.content:
A common pattern for official libraries is:
Install and wire dependencies via Plugin API (init({ plugins: [...] })).
Use Library API at runtime for domain events and transport wrappers.
This separation keeps boot lifecycle concerns out of your domain event model.

sections.heading: Authentication Modes
sections.content:
auth.mode defines how players are identified and authenticated on connection.
Identity supports three authentication modes:
local: authenticate using FiveM identifiers (license/steam/discord/etc.)
credentials: authenticate with username/password stored in your backend
api: delegate authentication to an external HTTP service
All modes are consumed through AuthService, which selects the correct provider based on configuration.

sections.heading: local (Default)
sections.content:
Authenticate using player identifiers (license/steam/discord/etc.). Ideal for classic FiveM servers where players simply join and play.
Workflow
Player connects.
Identity reads the primaryIdentifier from the player identifiers.
IdentityStore is queried for an account matching that identifier.
If missing and autoCreate=true, a new account is created and linked.

sections.heading: credentials
sections.content:
Username/password authentication stored in your system (passwords are hashed with bcrypt).
Workflow
Player registers via your event/command/UI.
Credentials are stored (hashed).
Player logs in using credentials on next sessions.

sections.heading: api
sections.content:
Delegates auth to your external HTTP service. Useful for networks with centralized accounts/SSO.
Workflow
Identity sends identifiers credentials to your API.
Your API returns { success, accountId, account?, isNewAccount? }.
Identity links the returned account to the player.

sections.heading: Principal Modes (Authorization)
sections.content:
principal.mode defines how Identity resolves the player's principal (role/rank/permissions).
Identity supports:
roles: static roles defined in code
db: roles loaded from your database using RoleStore
api: roles resolved by an external HTTP service

sections.heading: roles (Static)
sections.content:
Roles are defined in your Identity.install() options.
Best for
predefined staff/user roles
fast setup
minimal infrastructure

sections.heading: db (Dynamic)
sections.content:
Roles are resolved from a database through RoleStore. Identity caches results using cacheTtl.
Setup
Register RoleStore via Identity.setRoleStore().
Use principal.mode = "db".

sections.heading: api (External)
sections.content: Principal resolution is delegated to your API. Your API returns principal data such as rank, permissions, and optional metadata.

sections.heading: Permission Resolution Rules
sections.content:
Identity merges permissions using a strict priority:
Explicit Revocation: -permission denies access even if the role grants it.
Explicit Grant: +permission or permission grants access.
Wildcard Override: grants access.
Role Permissions: falls back to role permissions (supports ).
This allows precise per-account overrides without modifying global roles.

sections.heading: Implementing Contracts (Stores)
sections.content:
Identity is stateless by design: persistence is implemented through contracts.
You must implement:
IdentityStore (required): accounts, identifiers, bans, credential lookups
RoleStore (optional): only required when principal.mode = "db"

create(data)

title: Plugin API Usage
description: Install-time runtime extension model for OpenCore server and client.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Plugin API is OpenCore's install-time extension system.
It is designed for libraries that need to:
register services into DI,
expose runtime API extensions,
read init configuration,
and hook into framework bootstrap in a predictable order.
Unlike dynamic plugin ecosystems, OpenCore plugins are compile-time integrated and installed explicitly in init().

sections.heading: Entry Points and Boundaries
sections.content:
Server plugins: @open-core/framework/server
Client plugins: @open-core/framework/client
Plugin contracts are intentionally not exposed from @open-core/framework root.

sections.heading: Client
sections.content: Plugins are installed before full runtime bootstrap, so decorators and services can rely on plugin-provided extensions.

sections.heading: Extending Server and Client API
sections.content:
Use registerApiExtension to attach runtime features directly to the namespace object. Runtime usage is flat:
NPC(...)
Widget(...)
Not nested usage like ServerPluginApi.NPC(...).

sections.heading: Safety Guarantees
sections.content:
registerApiExtension enforces:
non-empty extension keys,
reserved key protection,
duplicate key protection,
no overwrite of existing API members.
These checks prevent plugin collisions and accidental runtime overrides.

sections.heading: Plugin API vs Library API
sections.content:
Use Plugin API for boot-time wiring and runtime extension.
Use Library API for domain events and runtime communication contracts.
Most production libraries combine both: plugin install for setup, library events for domain flow.

title: Command Execution

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The CommandExecutionPort handles the registration and routing of chat commands. Note: Most developers should use the @Command() decorator instead of interacting with this port directly. This port is considered an internal infrastructure component used by the framework to bridge commands across resources.

sections.heading: Key Features
sections.content:
Global Discovery: Commands can be registered in any resource but are collected by the Core.
Positional Execution: When a command is typed, the Core finds which resource owns it and routes the execution back to that resource.

sections.heading: getAllCommands()
sections.content: Returns a list of all commands registered across the entire framework, including their descriptions and usage strings. Useful for building Help Menus or Command Lists.

sections.heading: execute()
sections.content: Manually triggers a command execution for a player. This is more "internal" and used when the framework needs to simulate a player typing a command.

sections.heading: Decorator Integration
sections.content:
This port is the engine behind:
@Command('name', ...): When you use this decorator, the framework calls commandExecutionPort.register() during bootstrap.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
This port is essential for creating custom "Command List" UIs or help menus.
It ensures that even if a command is defined in a remote resource, the Core can still "see" it for permission validation.
Internal vs Public: Direct registration via this port is discouraged; prefer the declarative @Command() approach.

title: Introduction to Ports

sections.heading: What is a Port?
sections.content: In OpenCore, a Port is an architectural boundary that defines a contract for a core service. It follows the Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters) pattern. Ports allow the framework to remain mode-agnostic. This means your code can interact with "Core" functionality (like player directories or permissions) without knowing how or where that data is stored.

sections.heading: 1. The Core-Side Boundary
sections.content:
The primary problem Ports solve is the Resource vs. Core isolation. In FiveM, code usually runs in isolated resources. If you are writing a Core resource, the data is local (in memory).
If you are writing a Gameplay resource, the data belongs to the Core and must be accessed via exports or network events.
Ports abstract this away. When you inject a Port, the framework automatically provides the correct implementation based on the environment:
In the Core, it provides a Local Adapter (direct acce

sections.heading: 2. Why use Ports instead of Services?
sections.content: While Services handle business logic, Ports handle Framework Infrastructure. Feature Service Port Logic Specific (Vehicles, Chat) General (Sessions, Permissions) Location Defined in any resource Defined by the Framework Core Access Local to the resource Cross-resource (Remote access) Injection Via @Service() Via abstract class injection

sections.heading: 3. How it works (Remote Access)
sections.content:
When you ask for a Port in a resource that isn't the Core:
The framework detects it's in RESOURCE mode.
it injects a "Proxy" implementation of the Port.
Every method call you make is automatically routed to the Core resource.
The result is returned to your resource as if it were local.

sections.heading: 4. Key Ports available
sections.content:
Players: Access to active player sessions and metadata.
Authorization Port: Access to permissions, ranks, and authorization.
CommandExecutionPort: Registration and routing of chat commands.
PlayerSessionLifecyclePort: Creating and destroying sessions (Core-only).
--
:::info
Use ports when you need framework-level boundaries across runtime modes. For gameplay-focused operations, prefer the APIs listed under the Gameplay section.
:::

title: Player Directory

sections.heading: Description
sections.content:
The Players is the authoritative way to query information about players currently connected to the server. It provides a consistent interface to find players by their FiveM Client ID (source), Account ID, or to retrieve all active sessions.
This port is highly recommended for gameplay logic when you need to interact with other players (e.g., finding nearby players, getting a player's job, etc.).

sections.heading: getByClient()
sections.content: Returns the Player entity associated with a FiveM source ID. --

sections.heading: getAll()
sections.content:
Returns an array of all Player entities currently on the server.
--

sections.heading: getMeta() / setMeta()
sections.content: Accesses transient session metadata. This is data that exists only while the player is connected and is not saved to the database (e.g., "iscarryingobject", "currentblipid").

sections.heading: Internal vs. Public Use
sections.content:
Public (Gameplay): Use getByClient, getAll, and getMeta to drive your resource's logic. It is the safest way to access player data across resources.
Internal (Framework): Metadata management (setMeta) is often used by other services to track state without polluting the database.

sections.heading: Mode Behavior
sections.content:
CORE Mode: Accesses the local session map directly (O(1) performance).
RESOURCE Mode: Requests the data from the Core resource via exports.

title: Authorization Port

sections.heading: Description
sections.content:
The Authorization port is the gateway to the framework's security system. It allows you to query a player's Principal (permissions and rank) and enforce access control.
While you can use this port directly, it is most commonly used through the @Guard() decorator, which automatically invokes enforce().

sections.heading: hasPermission()
sections.content: Checks if a player has a specific permission string (supports wildcards like admin.). --

sections.heading: hasRank()
sections.content: Checks if a player's rank is equal to or higher than the required level. --

sections.heading: enforce()
sections.content: The primary method for security. It validates requirements and throws an error if the player is unauthorized. This method is what @Guard() uses under the hood. --

sections.heading: getPrincipal()
sections.content: Retrieves the full Principal object, including all permissions, rank, and role names.

sections.heading: Decorator Integration

title: Player Session Lifecycle

sections.heading: Description
sections.content:
The PlayerSessionLifecyclePort is an internal framework port responsible for managing the creation and destruction of player sessions.
Warning: This port should never be used in gameplay resources. It is exclusively for the Framework Core or specialized authentication resources that manage the low-level connection of players.

sections.heading: bind()
sections.content: Creates a new Player session and adds it to the internal registry. This is typically called during the initial connection handshake. --

sections.heading: unbind()
sections.content: Terminates a player session, removing them from the registry and freeing associated memory. This must be called when a player disconnects.

sections.heading: Internal Implementations
sections.content: OpenCore provides two distinct implementations of this port depending on where the code is running:

sections.heading: 1. PlayerService (Core Implementation)
sections.content:
Located in services/core, this is the Authoritative Implementation.
Mode: CORE / STANDALONE.
Behavior: Directly manages the Map<number, Playerin memory. It is responsible for creating the physical Player objects and injecting the necessary adapters (network, entity, etc.).

sections.heading: 2. RemotePlayerService (Remote Implementation)
sections.content:
Located in services/remote, this is the Proxy Implementation.
Mode: RESOURCE.
Behavior: Delegates all operations to the CORE resource via exports. When you call bind() or unbind() from a gameplay resource, it transparently notifies the Core to perform the actual operation.

sections.heading: Why this separation?
sections.content: In FiveM, multiple resources cannot share raw memory objects easily. By using this Port system: Uniform API: You write code against the PlayerSessionLifecyclePort without knowing if you are in the Core or a remote resource. State Consistency: The framework ensures that there is only one "Source of Truth" for player sessions (the Core), while allowing other resources to interact with them as if they were local.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
Automatic Handling: Most developers will never need to call these methods manually. The framework handles the lifecycle automatically via FiveM events (playerJoining, playerDropped).
Memory Safety: unbind() is critical to prevent memory leaks in the Core resource.

title: Command Error Observer

sections.heading: Description
sections.content:
The CommandErrorObserverContract is a global observer invoked whenever a command execution fails. It provides a centralized hook to react to command errors without coupling error handling logic to individual commands or controllers.
The framework does not notify players automatically when a command fails. Instead, it emits a rich error context and delegates the responsibility to this observer.

sections.heading: When is this observer called?
sections.content:
The observer is triggered whenever a command fails at any point in the execution pipeline:
Command dispatch (command not found)
Authentication failures
Security checks (@Guard, @Throttle, @RequiresState)
Argument validation (schema or type mismatch)
Command handler execution errors
Unexpected internal errors

sections.heading: Error Stages
sections.content: The stage field indicates where the error occurred: Stage Description -- -- dispatch Command not found or not routable auth Authentication failure security Guard, throttle, or security violations validation Schema or argument validation failures handler Error thrown inside the command handler unknown Fallback for uncategorized errors

sections.heading: Example: Notifying players on validation errors
Default Behavior
sections.content:
OpenCore ships with a DefaultCommandErrorObserver that:
Logs errors using the command logger
Never notifies the player
Never throws or interrupts execution

sections.heading: Safety Guarantees
sections.content:
Errors inside onError() are caught and logged as fatal
Command execution flow is never affected by observer failures
Observers are treated as user-land code and cannot break the framework

sections.heading: Common Use Cases
sections.content:
Custom player-facing error messages
Centralized logging and telemetry
Admin command auditing
Anti-abuse detection
Debug tooling in development mode

title: Input Validation (Zod Schemas)

sections.heading: Why Validation Matters
sections.content:
All external input should be validated before business logic runs.
Use Zod schemas with decorators to validate and coerce payloads consistently.

sections.heading: Net Events and RPC
sections.content:
OnNet(event, schema) validates client payloads.
OnRPC(action, { schema }) validates request payloads.
Use small, explicit schemas per endpoint.

sections.heading: Best Practices
sections.content:
Prefer coercion (z.coerce.number()) for chat/string inputs.
For @Command(..., z.object(...)), keep schema keys aligned with handler parameter names.
Keep schemas close to handlers for readability.
Reject unknown fields for sensitive objects.
Combine validation with Guard and Throttle on critical handlers.

title: Net Event Security Observer

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The NetEventSecurityObserverContract provides hooks to monitor and react to invalid payloads sent via network events. This is particularly useful for detecting automated exploitation attempts or malformed data from the client.

sections.heading: onInvalidPayload()
sections.content: Called when a network event receives a payload that doesn't match its expected schema (e.g., failed Zod validation) or has an incorrect argument count.

sections.heading: Context Data
sections.content:
The ctx object provides detailed information about the failure:
event — The name of the event that failed.

expectedArgsCount / receivedArgsCount.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.content:
If no observer is registered, the framework uses an internal default that logs violations silently.
This observer is ideal for building anti-cheat or anti-exploit detection layers.

title: Security Overview

sections.heading: Security Model
sections.content:
OpenCore applies security in the execution pipeline, not as an afterthought.
Core layers:
Access control (Guard, principals, permissions/ranks)
Throttling (Throttle and RateLimiterService)
State constraints (RequiresState)
Input validation (Zod schemas in commands/events/RPC)
Security observers/handlers for auditing and reactions

sections.heading: Default Behavior
sections.content:
Required security boundaries fail fast when misconfigured.
Optional observers have safe defaults.
Unauthorized execution is blocked before your handler logic runs.

sections.heading: Recommended Baseline
sections.content:
Define strict schemas for command/event inputs.
Use Guard on sensitive handlers.
Add Throttle for spam-prone endpoints.
Implement custom security handler/observers for logging and policy.

sections.heading: Description
sections.content: The SecurityHandlerContract allows you to define custom actions when a security violation occurs. A violation happens when a player fails a @Guard() check, attempts to use an unauthorized command, or triggers a rate limit.

title: Template Manifests

sections.heading: oc.manifest.json
sections.content:
OpenCore templates can publish metadata through an oc.manifest.json file placed at the root of the template directory.
Examples:
resources/xchat/oc.manifest.json
standalones/utils/oc.manifest.json
core/oc.manifest.json
This manifest lets the ecosystem describe what a template is, which runtimes it supports, and what other templates it depends on.

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.content:
The manifest solves two problems:
It gives template authors a clear place to declare compatibility.
It lets the CLI make smarter decisions when listing or cloning templates.
With manifests in place:
opencore clone --list can show compatibility information.
opencore clone <templatecan warn or block when the current project runtime does not match.
editors can validate manifests using the published JSON Schema.

sections.content: Place the manifest in the root of the template folder:

sections.content:

This allows the manifest format to evolve later without breaking existing templates.

sections.heading: compatibility
sections.content: Describes where the template is expected to work.

Allowed values:

This is the primary compatibility signal used by the CLI.

Allowed values:

Use this when the template logic is shared but still tied to a game family.
Examples:

List of template names this template expects.
Typical example:

sections.heading: links
sections.content: Optional documentation links.

sections.heading: Clone behavior
sections.content:
If a template publishes oc.manifest.json:
opencore clone --list shows compatibility labels
opencore clone <templatevalidates runtime compatibility against the current project when opencore.config.ts is available
opencore clone --force bypasses compatibility enforcement
Templates without a manifest remain supported and are treated as compatibility unknown.

sections.heading: Best practices
sections.content:
always set $schema to the public schema URL
keep name stable once published
declare only runtimes you actually support
use common only when the implementation is truly shared
add requires.templates when the template depends on core or another published template
keep description short and specific

sections.heading: Publishing and hosting
sections.content:
The canonical schema lives at https://opencorejs.dev/schemas/oc-manifest.schema.json.
In this docs site, that file is served from Docusaurus static assets:
source: static/schemas/oc-manifest.schema.json
public URL: /schemas/oc-manifest.schema.json
When the schema changes:
update the source copy in the CLI repository
sync the file into opencore-docs/static/schemas/oc-manifest.schema.json
deploy the docs site

title: Why OpenCore?

sections.heading: The Vision
sections.content:
OpenCore is designed to solve the structural problems that have plagued multiplayer server development for years: spaghetti code, lack of testability, and tight coupling between resources.
By bringing modern software engineering patterns (Inversion of Control, Hexagonal Architecture, and Type-Safety) to the world of GTA V modding, we enable developers to build complex, maintainable, and high-performance game servers.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Integrity
sections.content: Stop writing global variables and nested callbacks. OpenCore enforces a clean separation between your business logic (Services), your entry points (Controllers), and the underlying game engine (Adapters/Ports).

sections.heading: 2. True Modularity
sections.content: In FiveM, resources usually talk to each other via raw strings and events. OpenCore uses Ports and Adapters to provide type-safe, compiled interfaces across resources. If you change a method name in the Core, your other resources will fail at compile time, not runtime.

sections.heading: 3. Developer Productivity
sections.content:
Dependency Injection: Focus on logic, let the framework handle object instantiation.
Declarative Programming: Use decorators (@Command, @Guard) to describe what your code should do, not how to wire it up.
Dev Mode: Real-time feedback loops with Hot Reload and Player Simulation.

sections.heading: 4. Scalability
sections.content: OpenCore is built for large-scale servers. From the built-in rate limiter to the optimized parallel processing service, the framework is designed to handle hundreds of players and complex interactions without breaking a sweat.

sections.heading: Is it for me?
sections.content: If you are tired of debugging nil values in Lua, fighting with inconsistent exports, or maintaining thousands of lines of unorganized code, OpenCore is for you. It's not just a library; it's a foundation for the next generation of multiplayer game servers.
